chapter: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
title: Adolphus Osborne, the bass player who quit Duke
summary: A Kansas City bass player who left Duke Ellington because he disliked the harmonies and later taught in Minnesota.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, I lived in Kansas. See, I was raised and lived in Kansas when I was working with McShann, and worked over in Missouri with him.
And it was nothing. In fact, that bass player that preceded Blanton with Duke--he's from Kansas City. Remember the one that complained that Duke was using all the wrong chords and everything?
Now he was from Kansas City.
He was supposed to be a great bass player, wasn't he?

He was great, but he didn't want to consider that Duke was creatin' a new sound in music. He was great on his bass, and he was a great arranger in (like it) bands, you know, but he didn't want to concede those changes that Duke had, that sound.
What did he--what happened to him, then?
You know, he became a professor at the University of Missouri, Minnesota, University of Minnesota.
Well, maybe this was his trouble, that he was sort of todet legitimate in his thinking.
Evidently, it had to be that, 'cause I think he's the only guy who quit Duke. Everybody else wanted to get with him.
Yeah. He wasn't with Duke long, was he?

No, very short. And so, we understood. But what I meant to say about him was that Kansas City, Kansas was so close to Kansas City, Missouri that he'd play over in Kansas City, Missouri, and you'd see him walking across the viaduct with his bass on his back.
